10032511:
February 10, 2025
RE: Testimony in Opposition to LD 173 - An Act to Exempt Certain Watercraft from Registration Requirements
Dear Chair Baldacci, Chair Roberts, and members of the Inland Fisheries and Wildlife Committee,
As Executive Director of Lake Stewards of Maine (LSM), a statewide community lake science organization, I am asking the Committee to Oppose LD 173 - An Act to Exempt Certain Watercraft from Registration Requirements.
Maine's lakes and rivers are among our state's most valuable natural resources, supporting local economies, recreation, and wildlife. A critical source of funding in protecting these waters from aquatic invasive species (AIS) comes from the Lake and River Protection Sticker, which has been directly tied to the boat registration process. LSM is concerned that by exempting a significant number of boats from registering, the fallout will include the loss of Sticker sales and hence funding for valuable aquatic invasive species work.
Non-government organizations (NGO) such as LSM, rely on funding from the Lake and River Protection Sticker to support local lake associations and volunteer efforts in preventing and reducing the spread of aquatic invasive species (AIS). LSM has trained over 5,000 volunteers to survey lakes for AIS with the primary AIS goal of prevention and early detection. As a member of the state's AIS Rapid Response Team, we also assist lakes facing new invasive plant infestations mobilizing volunteers to conduct comprehensive surveys to determine the extent of an infestation. This work includes assisting communities in resource limited areas of the state struggling with AIS infestation. To complete this work, LSM depends on not only grants and donations, but also support from the Lake and River Protection Sticker sales. Reduction in Sticker revenue jeopardizes not only LSM's AIS prevention work, but the efforts of volunteers, lake associations and other lake-focused NGOs.
Funds generated from the Lake and River Protection Sticker help train and equip our dedicated volunteer invasive plant patrollers, whose contributions in volunteer hours multiply the impact of these funds tenfold. Even if the sticker remains a requirement, without the registration process to ensure purchase, enforcement will be nearly impossible. This could lead to a reduction in funding for aquatic invasive species prevention, early detection, and mitigation, ultimately increasing the risk of costly and damaging infestations in Maine's waters.
For these reasons, I urge you to vote Ought Not to Pass on LD 173. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,
Alison Cooney, LSM Executive Director alison@lakestewardsme.org

Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony in OPPOSITION to LD 173, which exempts canoes, kayaks, and rowboats with up to 100 HP motors from requiring registration.

Cross Lake is a high-risk lake for invasive aquatic species, especially lake-destroying Zebra mussels, which were recently discovered less than 30 miles away in the St. John River! Dakota Stankowski, Aquatic Invasive Species Coordinator at the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife (IF&W) was hired with funds from the increased Lake & River Protection Sticker Program. 183652:
TESTIMONY OF THE
DEPARTMENT OF INLAND FISHERIES AND WILDLIFE
BEFORE THE JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE ON INLAND FISHERIES AND WILDLIFE
In Opposition to L.D. 173
u - -- - n
An Act to Exempt Certam Watercraft from Registration Requirements
Sponsored by Representative WOOD of Greene.
Cosponsored by Representatives: DRINKWATER of Milford, MASON of Lisbon, THORNE of
Carmel.
DATE OF HEARING: February 10, 2025
Good afternoon, Senator Baldacci, Representative Roberts and members of the Inland Fisheries and Wildlife Committee. I am Dan Scott, Colonel of the Maine Warden Service, speaking on behalf of the Department, as well as the Department of Environmental Protection, (MDEP) in opposition to L.D. 173 An Act to Exempt Certain Watercraft from Registration Requirements.
As proposed, this bill would exempt canoes, kayaks and rowboats having a manufacturer's horsepower rating less than 100 Hp from the requirement of obtaining a certificate of number
from the Commissioner of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife. This certificate of number, commonly
known as a boat registration number, allows for watercraft identification that assists with
enforcement action for watercraft involved in unsafe or illegal activities. Registration also creates an avenue for education on safe practices and boating regulation compliance, and the
Department's Information & Education Division regularly sends relevant information and
targeted campaigns to the boating public through traditional media, social media, and targeted
emails.
In addition, the Lake and River Protection fee that is collected along with the boat registration fee provides funding for programs within the Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife (MDIFW) and the MDEP. Since 2002, the Lake and River Protection sticker has been required for all motorized watercraft operating on inland waters and funds the prevention, control and
eradication of invasive species infestations, which are usually associated with human activities
and carried by boats, trailers and associated equipment.
Exempting all canoes, kayaks, and rowboats equipped with a motor of 100 horsepower or less will lead to a significant reduction in revenue. This exemption would result in the removal of approximately 3,800 motorized canoe and kayak registrations, in addition to nearly 28,000 motorized rowboats (open motorboats).

When a resident registers a motorboat at their town office it triggers several revenue streams.
The town charges the registrant an excise tax based on an estimated value of the boat (not
unlike your MV excise tax). For first time boat registrants, the town also collects sales tax, which
is ultimately distributed (through the MOSES system) to the state's general fund. The registrant
pays the fee to register the motorboat, and if that motorboat is going to be used on inland waters it includes an additional Lake and River Protection program fee.
The revenue from the resident motorboat registration fee is first broken down to cover
administrative costs for the Department's Division of Licensing and Registration ($2.59 per registration). The remainder is distributed to the State General Fund to be appropriated as
follows: 75% to the MDIFW and 25% to the Department of Marine Resources.
As noted above, the resident registrations of a motorboat used on inland waters also includes the fee associated with the Lake and River Protection program. This Lake and River Protection
program fee generates revenue that is credited 30% to the MDIFW and 70% to MDEP for
invasive species prevention and control.
Nonresidents motorboats which are registered in another state have reciprocity with Maine. So, visiting boaters are not required to register their motorboats in Maine. However, they must still purchase the Lake and River Protection sticker separately if operating on inland waters.
Fees that support aquatic invasive species prevention and control program recently saw an increase to $25 that began January 1, 2025 and will see an additional $10 increase, up to $35 will begin on January 1, 2028. This is up from the prior $15 fee and is a result of Public Law 2023
Chapter 612. While MDIFW and MDEP jointly testified neither for nor against on L.D. 1342 and
recognize that the increased fee may disproportionately impact owners of multiple small,
motorized watercraft, both Departments have expanded the scope of their invasive aquatic species programs for the upcoming years due to the increase in revenue. Since the law passed, our agency has been building this program and any change to that would impact our ability to meet the expectations set by the Legislature.
MDIFW consulted with MDEP and if the bill passed the biggest impact on their agency would be
the reduced revenue from the Lake and River Protection fee. The MDEP's AIS Program conducted a strategic planning process in 2023-24 that identified goals including increasing support to lake groups, expanding program reach to areas of the state with little prevention and
plant survey activity, limiting new invasive aquatic plant infestations, and strengthening the
response to infestations. The approved revenue increases will fortify the boat inspection program, measures to detect invasive aquatic plants before they become established, and State and lake association efforts to manage existing infestations of invasive plants. The increases will also allow additional program support to areas like Rangeley, Moosehead, the County, and Downeast with currently limited capacity to prevent, detect and respond to infestations.

In addition to the loss of revenue for the MDIFW and the MDEP, the Maine Warden Service also
receives a grant through the United States Coast Guard (USCG) Recreational Boating Safety Program, that in part is allocated as a function of the number of registered vessels within the
state. Typically, we register between 120,000 -- 124,000 motorboats each year. The proposed bill would cause an approximate 26% reduction in the number of registered vessels within the
state that would be considered for grant allocation from the USCG Recreational Boating Safety Program. This would be another significant reduction in revenue for the agency, specifically for
boating enforcement.
*Note -- (The 26% is a rough estimate based on USCG data for motorboat types which only capture the length of the boat and do not reflect the horsepower which is how Maine determines the cost of the registration. The figure was based upon boats <14' (rowboats) in
length and registered as less than 100 Hp.)
Registration Fees (*Fee includes the registration, Lake and River Protection fee, and the $1.00 agent
fee.) This does not include sales tax or excise tax that may be charged.
A portion of each inland boat registration fee goes to the Lake and River protection program to help
protect Maine's waters from aquatic invasive species.

Members of the Inland Fisheries and Wildlife Committee:
I write in opposition to the proposed changes outlined in LD 173 that would exempt motorized watercraft with less than 100 HP from requirements for registration.

183651:
Testimony of Peter Lidiak Before the Committee on Inland Fisheries and Wildlife
On Behalf of the Cobbosseecontee Lake Association IN OPPOSITION to LD 173 An Act to Exempt Certain Watercraft from Registration Requirements
2/10/2025
Good afternoon, Chair Baldacci, Chair Roberts, and distinguished members of the committee.
My name is Peter Lidiak. I am a resident of Monmouth, ME and here today representing the
Cobbosseecontee Lake Association (CLA).
The mission of CLA is to serve as proactive stewards of our lake committed to protecting and improving all aspects of water quality, lake beauty, wildlife, and enjoyment of the lake for current and future generations.
CLA opposes LD 173 because it proposes to exempt from registration fees kayaks, canoes and row boats with motors rated less than 100 horsepower. Registration fees contribute to State safety, resource management, and environmental protection programs, including boating safety checks, the inspection of boats being launched on and mitigation of invasive species that have taken root in our state waters.
After 30 years of improved water quality, Lake Cobbosseecontee is facing the introduction of Eurasian Milfoil in multiple locations, in addition to at least two other invasive species. Any vessel with a motor poses the threat of carrying pieces of invasive plant life into our waterways.
So even the owners of smaller vessels that come onto our lakes and streams should pay
registration fees if they are using motors.

10032545:
Letter of OPPOSITION to LD 173 An Act to Exempt Certain Watercraft from Registration Requirements Submitted to Inland Fisheries and Wildlife Committee February 10, 2025
February 10, 2025
Dear Chair Baldacci, Chair Roberts, and Distinguished Members of the Inland Fisheries and Wildlife Committee [Recipient's Name]
I am writing to express my strong opposition to LD 173 An Act to Exempt Certain Watercraft from Registration Requirements that seeks to remove the requirement for boat registration for boats with less than 100 horsepower (HP). As a concerned resident, avid boater and fisherman, I believe that this proposal poses significant risks to our community, our environment, and the overall safety of our waterways. As an active boater and fisherman, preserving our lakes and waterways for all to use today and in the future is essential to the "Way Life should Be".
First and foremost, boat registration serves as a critical tool for ensuring the safety and accountability of all boat operators. By requiring registration, authorities can easily track and identify boats, which is essential in case of accidents, theft, or violations of boating laws. Removing the need for registration for boats with less than 100 HP would create a loophole that could be exploited by irresponsible or reckless operators, leading to an increase in unregistered and untraceable boats on our waters. Registration is also a mechanism to insure that all operators are informed regarding the latest regulations for safe boating in Maine.
Furthermore, boat registration fees contribute to the maintenance and improvement of our state's boating infrastructure. These funds are used to maintain boat ramps, docks, and other facilities that are vital for the enjoyment and safety of all boaters. Without this source of revenue, the quality of our boating infrastructure could decline, negatively impacting recreational boating and water activities.
In addition to safety and infrastructure concerns, boat registration also plays a crucial role in environmental protection. Registered boats are subject to regulations and inspections that help prevent the spread of invasive species, pollution, and other environmental hazards. The registration process is a simple mechanism to ensure all boats have the required Lake and River Protection sticker. By exempting boats with less than 100 HP from registration, we risk undermining these important safeguards and endangering the health of our irreplaceable waterways and marine ecosystems.
Lastly, I believe that the proposed legislation would create confusion and inconsistency in the enforcement of boating laws. Law enforcement officers would face additional challenges in distinguishing between registered and unregistered boats, complicating their efforts to ensure compliance with safety and environmental regulations.
In conclusion, I urge you to vote NO on this proposed legislation and to maintain the requirement for boat registration for all boats, regardless of horsepower. The benefits of registration far outweigh any perceived convenience of eliminating it for smaller boats. Let us prioritize the safety, environmental

health, and overall well-being of our valuable lakes and boating community by upholding this essential regulation.
Thank you for considering my perspective on this important issue. I hope that you will take the necessary steps to protect our waterways and ensure the continued enjoyment of our exceptional lakes and waterways for all residents of Maine.
Sincerely,
Peter Tilkemeier 91 Pine Drive Otisfield, ME 04270
